note: agent-lifted from VC's manuals (pilot steps 2 and 3)

concepts.label: the digital cross-connect
concepts.gloss: A VC digital cross-connect is the network resource that digitally switches ODU connections between line modules and tributary interfaces and can suffer fabric, hardware, or provisioning faults.
concepts.example: A VC-DXC switches an ODU from a VC-WT-400D line module to a VC-TRIB-400 tributary port.

concepts.label: switches ODUs between line modules and tributaries
concepts.gloss: The digital-cross-connect switching function maps and transfers ODUs between optical line modules and customer-facing tributary interfaces.
concepts.example: The function takes an ODU arriving from a line module and switches it to the provisioned tributary.

concepts.label: tributary port
concepts.gloss: A tributary port is a customer-facing VC interface that terminates or originates client service, reports tributary faults, and measures customer errored and unavailable seconds.
concepts.example: A VC-TRIB-100 carries a 100-Gbit/s customer service and raises TRIB-FAIL when that service fails.

concepts.label: launch OFA
concepts.gloss: A launch optical fibre amplifier is the VC-OFA-T resource placed where a wavelength section leaves a wavelength router to establish outbound optical power.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-T amplifies the outgoing wavelength band before it enters the first fibre span.

concepts.label: where a wavelength section leaves the wavelength router
concepts.gloss: This is the egress boundary at a wavelength router where a routed wavelength section begins and enters its outbound optical path.
concepts.example: The launch OFA is installed between the router output and the fibre section leaving the site.

concepts.label: mid-span OFA
concepts.gloss: A mid-span optical fibre amplifier is a VC-OFA-M resource in a repeater shelter that restores optical power between terminal sites without terminating wavelengths.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-M in a shelter amplifies all wavelengths after an 80-km fibre span.

concepts.label: in repeater shelters between terminals
concepts.gloss: Repeater shelters are intermediate sites between terminals that house mid-span amplifiers and terminate and regenerate supervisory links for adjacent fibre spans.
concepts.example: A shelter halfway between two terminals contains a VC-OFA-M and starts a new supervisory link for the next span.

concepts.label: landing OFA
concepts.gloss: A landing optical fibre amplifier is the VC-OFA-R resource at the receiving end of a wavelength section, where that section arrives at the next router.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-R boosts wavelengths arriving from the line before they enter the destination wavelength router.

concepts.label: where a wavelength section arrives at the next wavelength router
concepts.gloss: This is the ingress boundary at the next wavelength router where an incoming wavelength section ends.
concepts.example: The landing OFA sits at the point where the intersite fibre section reaches the receiving router.

concepts.label: wavelength router
concepts.gloss: A wavelength router is a VC-WR-X optical resource that independently steers wavelengths between directions while monitoring each wavelength's level and OSNR.
concepts.example: A VC-WR-X routes wavelength λ7 from the west input to the south output and reports its optical level.

concepts.label: single-client wavelength terminal
concepts.gloss: A single-client wavelength terminal is a VC-WT-400T transponder that maps one client service onto one optical wavelength and terminates that wavelength at the far end.
concepts.example: A VC-WT-400T carries one 400-Gbit/s client over a dedicated wavelength.

concepts.label: aggregating wavelength terminal
concepts.gloss: An aggregating wavelength terminal combines several lower-rate client services onto one line wavelength and is realised by VC-WT-200A or VC-WT-400A equipment.
concepts.example: A VC-WT-400A aggregates four client ODUs into one 400-Gbit/s wavelength.

concepts.label: several clients on one wavelength
concepts.gloss: This denotes the aggregation arrangement in which multiple client services share the capacity of a single line wavelength.
concepts.example: Four 100-Gbit/s clients are multiplexed onto one 400-Gbit/s wavelength.

concepts.label: digital-switching line module
concepts.gloss: A digital-switching line module is a VC-WT-200D or VC-WT-400D terminal module that provides an optical wavelength interface to the digital cross-connect.
concepts.example: A VC-WT-400D receives an ODU from the VC-DXC and transmits it on a 400-Gbit/s line wavelength.

concepts.label: Fabric outage
concepts.gloss: A fabric outage is failure of a digital cross-connect's switching fabric that cuts every ODU switched through that cross-connect.
concepts.example: When the VC-DXC fabric loses power, all ODUs traversing it are interrupted together.

concepts.label: Mis-provisioned connection
concepts.gloss: A mis-provisioned connection is an incorrect digital cross-connect mapping that sends one ODU to the wrong destination while leaving the optical layer apparently normal.
concepts.example: An operator maps customer A's ODU to customer B's tributary, causing TRACE-MISMATCH without an optical alarm.

concepts.label: Tributary failure
concepts.gloss: A tributary failure is loss or malfunction of the customer-facing optic or tributary interface that causes the associated customer service to fail.
concepts.example: Failure of a VC-TRIB-100 optic drops its customer service and raises TRIB-FAIL.

concepts.label: any fault
concepts.gloss: Any fault is a deliberately non-specific probable-cause category used when an alarm indicates an affected route or service but does not identify the underlying defect.
concepts.example: ON-STANDBY may cite any fault because many unrelated primary-route failures can trigger protection switching.

concepts.label: tributary hardware fault
concepts.gloss: A tributary hardware fault is a physical equipment defect localized within the identified tributary port.
concepts.example: A failed component on VC-TRIB-400 raises TRIB-HW for that tributary.

concepts.label: fabric hardware fault
concepts.gloss: A fabric hardware fault is a physical defect within the specified digital cross-connect's switching fabric hardware.
concepts.example: A failed switching-fabric card in VC-DXC raises FABRIC-HW.

concepts.label: Amplifier outage
synonyms: the module is out of service
concepts.gloss: An amplifier outage is an OFA being out of service so that no optical signal leaves the module and all wavelengths it carried disappear.
concepts.example: Loss of power to a VC-OFA-M makes its output dark and removes every wavelength on the span.

concepts.label: Gain sag
concepts.gloss: Gain sag is an amplifier degradation in which actual optical gain falls below its intended value, making every carried wavelength weaker and noisier.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-R set for 20 dB gain delivers only 16 dB, lowering all output channels.

concepts.label: Excess noise
concepts.gloss: Excess noise is an amplifier impairment that worsens every wavelength's OSNR even though aggregate output levels can remain normal.
concepts.example: A faulty OFA preserves channel power but adds ASE noise, causing downstream OSNR to fall.

concepts.label: Pump wear-out
concepts.gloss: Pump wear-out is gradual ageing of an OFA pump that requires increasing drive current and ultimately reaches the PUMP-EOL threshold, usually before service is affected.
concepts.example: An amplifier's I-PUMP rises from 100% to 121% of commissioning value and raises PUMP-EOL.

concepts.label: Spectral tilt
concepts.gloss: Spectral tilt is unequal amplification across the optical band that leaves wavelengths at one band edge weaker than others.
concepts.example: Channels near the long-wavelength edge emerge 3 dB below the centre channels.

concepts.label: a severed fibre
concepts.gloss: A severed fibre is a complete physical break in an optical span that prevents signal and supervisory light from reaching the downstream equipment.
concepts.example: Excavation cuts the intersite cable, causing IN-DARK and SV-LOSS at the next shelter.

concepts.label: fibre attenuation that has jumped
concepts.gloss: An attenuation jump is a sudden increase in fibre-path loss that sharply reduces or extinguishes received optical power.
concepts.example: A bent cable adds 12 dB of loss and causes the downstream amplifier input to go dark.

concepts.label: an unplugged patch lead
concepts.gloss: An unplugged patch lead is a disconnected local optical jumper that opens the wavelength path at a terminal or section head.
concepts.example: A technician removes the launch-site patch cord, and the landing OFA raises SEC-IN-DARK.

concepts.label: Over-attenuation
concepts.gloss: Over-attenuation is wavelength-specific loss beyond the router's compensation range, leaving that wavelength weak at the router output.
concepts.example: A channel arrives 12 dB low where the router can correct only 8 dB, so it exits weak.

concepts.label: Passband misalignment
concepts.gloss: Passband misalignment is incorrect alignment of a router filter to a wavelength, allowing normal measured level while clipping the signal and degrading quality.
concepts.example: A filter is offset from λ12, so λ12 has normal power but excessive pre-FEC errors.

concepts.label: Direction input fault
synonyms: a router input that has failed
concepts.gloss: A direction input fault is failure of one wavelength-router ingress direction that stops all light entering there while traffic from other directions continues.
concepts.example: Failure of the west input blocks every westbound incoming channel but leaves north-input channels operating.

concepts.label: Transmitter dark
concepts.gloss: A dark transmitter is a terminal failure in which the transmit laser stops producing optical light.
concepts.example: A VC-WT-400T laser shuts down, and the far-end terminal raises RX-DARK.

concepts.label: Module failure
concepts.gloss: A module failure is loss of a wavelength-terminal module that removes its transmitted and received traffic, stops telemetry, and masks traffic alarms behind a hardware alarm.
concepts.example: A failed VC-WT-400D card raises MOD-HW, stops telemetry, and loses both directions of its wavelength.

concepts.label: Receiver impairment
concepts.gloss: Receiver impairment is a defect local to one terminal receiver that creates errors there while the route and other wavelengths remain healthy.
concepts.example: A faulty coherent receiver reports high pre-FEC errors although OSNR and peer channels are normal.

concepts.label: Transmitter wear-out
concepts.gloss: Transmitter wear-out is progressive laser ageing evidenced by rising bias current and ending in a dark transmitter.
concepts.example: A terminal laser's bias climbs to 125% of commissioning value before it eventually fails.

concepts.label: Margin creep
concepts.gloss: Margin creep is a slow reduction in a wavelength's performance margin accumulated along its route and observed at the receiving terminal.
concepts.example: Over several months, estimated OSNR margin falls from 5 dB to 2 dB at the receiver.

concepts.label: DGD growth
concepts.gloss: DGD growth is an increase in differential group delay on a wavelength until polarization-mode dispersion degrades or destroys frame recovery.
concepts.example: Measured DGD rises from 8 ps to 35 ps and triggers DEGRADE at the terminal.

concepts.label: a polarisation swing
concepts.gloss: A polarisation swing is a rapid change in optical state of polarization that may outrun the receiver's tracking system.
concepts.example: A cable disturbance causes polarization to rotate faster than the coherent receiver can follow, producing frame loss.

concepts.label: a soiled connector end-face
concepts.gloss: A soiled connector end-face is contamination on an optical mating surface that introduces loss, reflection, or noise and degrades the wavelength.
concepts.example: Dust on a terminal connector raises pre-FEC errors until the end-face is cleaned.

concepts.label: transmit laser fault
concepts.gloss: A transmit laser fault is a hardware defect localized to the transmitter of the current wavelength terminal.
concepts.example: Failure of the laser driver in a VC-WT-400A raises TX-HW on that terminal.

concepts.label: Module hardware fault
concepts.gloss: A module hardware fault is a physical equipment failure localized within the current wavelength-terminal module.
concepts.example: A failed module processor raises MOD-HW and stops the card's telemetry.

concepts.label: receives an ODU AIS
synonyms: an ODU AIS is received on an ODU it switches
concepts.gloss: This condition means a tributary or cross-connect is receiving ODU Alarm Indication Signal on an ODU it handles, indicating an upstream failure replacement signal.
concepts.example: A VC-TRIB-100 receives ODU AIS from the network and raises AIS-IN.

concepts.label: passes an ODU AIS along on every ODU it switches
concepts.gloss: This condition means the digital cross-connect transparently forwards received ODU AIS on each affected switched ODU rather than terminating it.
concepts.example: AIS entering a VC-DXC on ODU2 is passed to the provisioned egress tributary.

concepts.label: receives an ODU meant for someone else
synonyms: the ODU arriving is not the expected one
concepts.gloss: This condition means the arriving ODU trace identifies a destination other than the one expected by the receiving tributary.
concepts.example: A tributary expecting customer A's trace receives customer B's ODU and raises TRACE-MISMATCH.

concepts.label: the customer service on this tributary has failed
concepts.gloss: This condition is loss of the customer service carried on the specified tributary, regardless of whether the cause is local, routed, or upstream.
concepts.example: The Ethernet service on VC-TRIB-400 drops and the port raises TRIB-FAIL.

concepts.label: the service is dual-homed, with a primary and a standby ODU route
concepts.gloss: This condition means a service has both a primary ODU route and a standby ODU route for protection.
concepts.example: A customer ODU is provisioned over route A with route B reserved as standby.

concepts.label: the selector is at the receiving tributary
concepts.gloss: This condition places the protection selector at the receiving tributary, where it chooses between primary and standby ODU inputs.
concepts.example: The destination VC-TRIB-100 selects whichever of the two incoming routes is healthy.

concepts.label: the standby route is clean
concepts.gloss: This condition means the standby ODU route is healthy and suitable for selection when the primary route fails.
concepts.example: Route B carries no AIS or defects, so the selector can switch to it.

concepts.label: the customer only sees a short interruption while the selector moves
concepts.gloss: This condition is the brief customer-visible traffic break that occurs while a protection selector changes from one ODU route to another.
concepts.example: A primary failure causes a 50-ms interruption before the receiving tributary selects standby.

concepts.label: dies
concepts.gloss: This condition is complete loss of operation of the switching fabric in the current cross-connect.
concepts.example: The fabric controller and switching matrix stop, so the VC-DXC can no longer switch ODUs.

concepts.label: is cut
concepts.gloss: This condition means every ODU traversing the failed cross-connect is interrupted by the fabric outage.
concepts.example: All 40 ODUs switched through the site drop simultaneously.

concepts.label: is set up wrongly
concepts.gloss: This condition means the logical cross-connect mapping for a connection has been provisioned incorrectly.
concepts.example: The ingress ODU is configured to the wrong egress port.

concepts.label: ends up at the wrong destination
concepts.gloss: This condition means one affected ODU is delivered to an endpoint other than its intended recipient.
concepts.example: Customer A's ODU arrives on customer B's tributary.

concepts.label: Nothing shows
concepts.gloss: This condition means an ODU provisioning error has no corresponding symptom on the optical transport side because optical power and wavelengths remain present.
concepts.example: The wavelength remains healthy even though the DXC maps the ODU to the wrong tributary.

concepts.label: fails
concepts.gloss: This condition means the customer-facing optic or the tributary interface itself has ceased to provide its intended service.
concepts.example: A failed tributary receiver can no longer deliver the customer's signal.

concepts.label: the other end says it is receiving ODU AIS
concepts.gloss: This condition means the far endpoint reports that it is receiving ODU AIS from the local direction.
concepts.example: The local tributary raises REMOTE-AIS after the peer reports AIS on the ODU sent to it.

concepts.label: the selector has moved to the standby route
concepts.gloss: This condition means the receiving protection selector is currently forwarding traffic from the standby ODU route.
concepts.example: After route A fails, the selector chooses route B and ON-STANDBY is raised.

concepts.label: the standby route has failed
concepts.gloss: This condition means the configured standby ODU route is unavailable or defective and cannot provide protection.
concepts.example: Route B begins receiving AIS, causing STANDBY-LOST while traffic remains on route A.

concepts.label: At installation
concepts.gloss: This is the commissioning-time context in which an amplifier's reference gain and drive values are established.
concepts.example: At installation, the technician records pump drive as the 100% reference.

concepts.label: the gain is set to cancel the attenuation of the fibre length that feeds the module
concepts.gloss: This condition means an OFA's gain is commissioned to offset the attenuation of the fibre span feeding it.
concepts.example: For a span measured at 18 dB loss, the receiving OFA is set to 18 dB gain.

concepts.label: the module keeps that gain from then on
concepts.gloss: This condition means the OFA subsequently maintains its commissioned gain rather than automatically compensating for later upstream power changes.
concepts.example: An OFA remains at 18 dB gain after the incoming signal falls by 3 dB.

concepts.label: When the incoming light weakens
concepts.gloss: This condition is a reduction in aggregate optical power entering an amplifier.
concepts.example: A fibre bend reduces the amplifier's input power by 4 dB.

concepts.label: the outgoing light weakens by the same amount
concepts.gloss: This condition means fixed-gain amplification causes output power to fall by the same amount as input power.
concepts.example: With gain unchanged, a 4-dB input drop produces a 4-dB output drop.

concepts.label: every wavelength carried gets noisier
concepts.gloss: This condition means all wavelengths transported through the affected path experience worsened signal-to-noise quality.
concepts.example: After input power falls, every channel downstream shows lower OSNR.

concepts.label: When the incoming light disappears
concepts.gloss: This condition is total loss of optical light at an amplifier's input.
concepts.example: A fibre cut makes the mid-span OFA input power fall below detection.

concepts.label: the outgoing light disappears too
concepts.gloss: This condition means an amplifier produces no carried optical output because its incoming light has vanished.
concepts.example: After the input fibre is cut, no wavelengths leave the otherwise operating OFA.

concepts.label: Anything else the module receives
concepts.gloss: This condition denotes non-supervisory optical traffic or information received by an intermediate amplifier module.
concepts.example: The module receives the full set of customer wavelengths in addition to the supervisory channel.

concepts.label: it sends on as it is
concepts.gloss: This condition means the module forwards received carried content transparently without terminating or altering it logically.
concepts.example: A mid-span OFA amplifies and forwards each customer wavelength unchanged.

concepts.label: Every shelter
concepts.gloss: This condition applies the stated supervisory-link behavior at each repeater shelter along the route.
concepts.example: Each of five shelters terminates the incoming supervisory span and originates the next one.

concepts.label: ends the supervisory link it receives
concepts.gloss: This condition means a repeater shelter terminates the supervisory communication link received over the preceding fibre span.
concepts.example: Shelter 3 receives and terminates the supervisory channel from shelter 2.

concepts.label: starts a fresh one on the next fibre length
concepts.gloss: This condition means a repeater shelter originates a new supervisory link for the following fibre span.
concepts.example: Shelter 3 starts a new supervisory channel toward shelter 4.

concepts.label: a supervisory outage
concepts.gloss: A supervisory outage is loss of management or monitoring communication over one amplifier-to-amplifier fibre span.
concepts.example: The supervisory channel fails between shelters 2 and 3 while adjacent supervisory spans remain up.

concepts.label: never spreads beyond the fibre length where it occurs
concepts.gloss: This condition means a supervisory-link failure remains confined to the fibre span on which it occurs because each shelter terminates and regenerates the link.
concepts.example: Loss between shelters 2 and 3 does not interrupt supervision between shelters 3 and 4.

concepts.label: nothing leaves the module
concepts.gloss: This condition is complete absence of optical output from the affected amplifier module.
concepts.example: An out-of-service VC-OFA-T emits no light on its line output.

concepts.label: is gone
concepts.gloss: This condition means all wavelengths formerly carried by the failed amplifier are absent downstream.
concepts.example: The eight channels through a failed OFA disappear at the next site.

concepts.label: leaves the module weaker
concepts.gloss: This condition means every wavelength exits the affected amplifier at a lower level than intended.
concepts.example: Gain sag lowers each output channel by 3 dB.

concepts.label: leaves the module noisier
concepts.gloss: This condition means every wavelength leaving the affected amplifier has poorer OSNR than intended.
concepts.example: A degraded pump causes all output channels to lose 1 dB of OSNR.

concepts.label: look normal
concepts.gloss: This condition means measured optical output powers remain within normal limits despite an underlying noise impairment.
concepts.example: Channel powers remain at -2 dBm while OSNR falls because of excess amplifier noise.

concepts.label: is noisier
concepts.gloss: This condition means each wavelength shows increased noise at downstream observation points.
concepts.example: Every channel measured at the next router has 2 dB lower OSNR.

concepts.label: creeps up
concepts.gloss: This condition is a gradual rise in the module's normalized I-PUMP value as the amplifier pump ages.
concepts.example: I-PUMP increases from 100% to 115% over two years.

concepts.label: ends in PUMP-EOL
concepts.gloss: This condition means the rising pump-drive trend eventually crosses the threshold that raises PUMP-EOL on the module.
concepts.example: The trend reaches 120% and the OFA reports PUMP-EOL.

concepts.label: no service effect until late
concepts.gloss: This condition means pump ageing initially leaves transported service unaffected until the degradation becomes advanced.
concepts.example: Traffic remains error-free while I-PUMP rises from 105% to 115%.

concepts.label: come out weaker
concepts.gloss: This condition means wavelengths at one edge of the optical band leave the amplifier below the level of the rest of the band.
concepts.example: The highest-frequency channels exit 2 dB weaker because of spectral tilt.

concepts.label: no light
concepts.gloss: This condition is absence of detectable optical signal at a receiving interface.
concepts.example: The terminal measures no receive power and raises RX-DARK.

concepts.label: receives nothing
concepts.gloss: This condition is absence of the expected supervisory signal at an OFA receiver.
concepts.example: A mid-span amplifier receives no supervisory channel from the preceding shelter and raises SV-LOSS.

concepts.label: no light although light is entering
concepts.gloss: This condition means an amplifier output is dark even though valid optical light is present at its input.
concepts.example: The OFA input measures -10 dBm but its output is absent, causing OUT-DARK.

concepts.label: the gain strays more than 2 dB from its setting
concepts.gloss: This condition occurs when an amplifier's actual gain differs from its configured gain by more than 2 dB.
concepts.example: An OFA configured for 18 dB delivers 15.5 dB and raises GAIN-DEV.

concepts.label: I-PUMP passes 120 per cent of its commissioning value
concepts.gloss: This condition occurs when normalized OFA pump drive exceeds 120 percent of its commissioning value.
concepts.example: I-PUMP reaches 121%, causing PUMP-EOL.

concepts.label: as it leaves a direction
concepts.gloss: This condition identifies the router egress stage at which an individually selected wavelength exits an input direction toward its chosen output.
concepts.example: Wavelength λ5 is independently steered as it leaves the west direction.

concepts.label: The router steers every wavelength on its own.
concepts.gloss: This condition means the wavelength router makes an independent forwarding decision for every wavelength rather than switching the input band as one unit.
concepts.example: The router sends λ1 south and λ2 east although both arrived from the west.

concepts.label: A problem hits all the light entering on one direction
concepts.gloss: This condition is an impairment shared by all optical light entering one router direction.
concepts.example: Failure of the west ingress attenuates every wavelength arriving from the west.

concepts.label: the problem reappears, after the router, on each wavelength steered onwards from it
concepts.gloss: This condition means a shared ingress-direction impairment remains observable after the router on every wavelength forwarded from that input.
concepts.example: Low OSNR on west-input channels is seen on both south and east outputs after routing.

concepts.label: as long as its attenuation range allows
concepts.gloss: This condition limits router level equalization to input loss that falls within the router's available attenuation or compensation range.
concepts.example: The router corrects a 6-dB drop because its equalization range is 8 dB.

concepts.label: brings the wavelength levels back to the launch level
concepts.gloss: This condition means the wavelength router equalizes outgoing channel powers back to their configured launch level.
concepts.example: A channel arriving 5 dB low is restored to the standard output level.

concepts.label: A drop in level of up to about 8 dB before the router
concepts.gloss: This condition is an upstream wavelength-level reduction of no more than about 8 dB before the router.
concepts.example: A channel loses 7 dB on the preceding span before entering the router.

concepts.label: is evened out at the router
concepts.gloss: This condition means the router compensates a within-range input-level drop so the wavelength leaves at normal launch power.
concepts.example: The router restores a channel from -9 dBm input to its normal -2 dBm output.

concepts.label: the noise penalty the drop caused does not go away
concepts.gloss: This condition means power equalization restores level but cannot remove the OSNR degradation caused by the preceding loss.
concepts.example: The router restores channel power, but the channel remains 3 dB worse in OSNR.

concepts.label: A bigger drop
concepts.gloss: This condition is an upstream wavelength-level reduction greater than the router can compensate.
concepts.example: A 12-dB loss exceeds an 8-dB equalization range.

concepts.label: leaves the router weak
synonyms: leaves the router as a weak wavelength
concepts.gloss: This condition means one wavelength leaves the router below its required output level because excessive attenuation could not be corrected.
concepts.example: After a 12-dB pre-router loss, λ8 exits the router 4 dB weak.

concepts.label: crosses the router as it arrived
concepts.gloss: This condition means a wavelength passes through the router with the impairment it already had on arrival.
concepts.example: A noisy channel retains its poor OSNR while being routed to the east output.

concepts.label: level is fine
concepts.gloss: This condition means the affected wavelength's measured optical power remains acceptable despite another quality impairment.
concepts.example: A passband-clipped channel measures -2 dBm, its expected level.

concepts.label: quality suffers
concepts.gloss: This condition means one wavelength has impaired signal quality, such as reduced OSNR or increased errors, despite adequate power.
concepts.example: The channel level is normal but pre-FEC errors rise sharply.

concepts.label: stops at the router
concepts.gloss: This condition means all optical light entering the failed router direction is blocked at that router.
concepts.example: A west-input fault prevents every west-arriving wavelength from leaving the router.

concepts.label: carries on
concepts.gloss: This condition means light arriving on unaffected router directions continues to be routed normally.
concepts.example: North-input channels remain in service while the west input has failed.

concepts.label: the terminal declares a loss-of-signal defect (dLOS in G.798 terms)
concepts.gloss: This condition means a terminal raises the G.798 loss-of-signal defect when it detects no usable incoming optical signal.
concepts.example: After a fibre cut, the receiver declares dLOS.

concepts.label: can no longer find its OTU frame
concepts.gloss: This condition means a receiving terminal cannot detect or synchronize to the expected OTU frame in the incoming signal.
concepts.example: Severe noise prevents the framer from locating OTU frame boundaries.

concepts.label: the terminal declares an equipment defect (dEQ)
concepts.gloss: This condition means a terminal raises the G.798 equipment defect when its own module hardware is unable to operate correctly.
concepts.example: A failed terminal card declares dEQ and raises MOD-HW.

concepts.label: the OTU frame is lost
concepts.gloss: This condition is loss of OTU frame synchronization at the receiving terminal.
concepts.example: The receiver has light but cannot maintain OTU framing and raises FRAME-LOSS.

concepts.label: Light that arrives in poor shape
concepts.gloss: This condition denotes received optical light whose power, noise, dispersion, filtering, or margin is inadequate for reliable decoding.
concepts.example: A channel arrives with low OSNR and excessive DGD even though light is present.

concepts.label: weak
concepts.gloss: This condition means received optical power is below the level required for reliable terminal operation.
concepts.example: The receiver sees -24 dBm where at least -18 dBm is required.

concepts.label: noisy
concepts.gloss: This condition means the optical signal has insufficient signal-to-noise ratio for reliable decoding.
concepts.example: OSNR falls to 10 dB and pre-FEC errors increase.

concepts.label: with too much differential group delay
concepts.gloss: This condition means differential group delay exceeds the receiver's tolerance.
concepts.example: DGD reaches 40 ps on a receiver rated for 25 ps.

concepts.label: clipped by a filter
concepts.gloss: This condition means part of a wavelength's modulation spectrum is cut off by a misaligned or overly narrow optical filter.
concepts.example: A shifted router passband removes one edge of the coherent signal spectrum.

concepts.label: spoiled by the receiver itself
concepts.gloss: This condition means otherwise usable incoming light is degraded by a fault inside the receiving terminal itself.
concepts.example: A defective receiver front end creates errors while an external analyzer shows a healthy signal.

concepts.label: with its margin slowly worn away
concepts.gloss: This condition means a wavelength's tolerance to additional impairment has been progressively consumed.
concepts.example: The channel margin falls from 6 dB to 1 dB after gradual route degradation.

concepts.label: pre-FEC errors begin once the damage exceeds the wavelength's margin
concepts.gloss: This condition means pre-FEC errors appear once accumulated impairment exceeds the wavelength's available performance margin.
concepts.example: When OSNR drops below the margin threshold, the terminal begins counting corrected bit errors.

concepts.label: the frame is lost once it exceeds the margin by far
concepts.gloss: This condition means OTU framing is lost when impairment exceeds the wavelength's margin by a large amount.
concepts.example: A further 6-dB OSNR loss turns a degraded channel into FRAME-LOSS.

concepts.label: Polarisation swings faster than the tracker can follow
concepts.gloss: This condition means polarization changes more rapidly than the coherent receiver's tracking loop can follow.
concepts.example: Fast polarization rotation causes bursts of uncorrectable errors and frame loss.

concepts.label: Once the OTU frame is gone
concepts.gloss: This condition marks the state after the receiving terminal has completely lost the OTU frame.
concepts.example: Following severe DGD, the framer transitions from high errors to no frame lock.

concepts.label: the terminal follows G.798
concepts.gloss: This condition means the terminal applies the G.798-defined defect and consequent-action behavior after OTU frame loss.
concepts.example: On frame loss, the terminal declares the prescribed defect and inserts downstream AIS.

concepts.label: It inserts ODU AIS towards every ODU it carries downstream
concepts.gloss: This condition means the terminal replaces affected downstream ODU payloads with ODU AIS after losing the upstream OTU frame.
concepts.example: A line terminal with FRAME-LOSS sends ODU AIS toward every carried tributary ODU.

concepts.label: returns a backward defect indication to the terminal at the other end
concepts.gloss: This condition means the terminal sends a backward defect indication to inform the far-end transmitter of a receive-side failure.
concepts.example: After losing the OTU frame, the receiver reports the defect back to the remote terminal.

concepts.label: The transmit laser stops or fails
concepts.gloss: This condition is cessation or failure of the terminal's transmit laser output.
concepts.example: The local laser emits zero power after its driver fails.

concepts.label: loses the wavelength this module sends
concepts.gloss: This condition means the remote terminal no longer receives the wavelength sent by the failed local module.
concepts.example: A local MOD-HW failure makes the far end lose the line wavelength and raise RX-DARK.

concepts.label: what the module receives is lost
concepts.gloss: This condition means all traffic received by the failed module is lost on the local side.
concepts.example: The module failure prevents locally received ODU traffic from reaching the DXC.

concepts.label: its telemetry stops
concepts.gloss: This condition means the failed module ceases reporting management measurements and status on the local side.
concepts.example: After MOD-HW, receive power and temperature updates stop.

concepts.label: its traffic alarms are hidden behind the hardware alarm
concepts.gloss: This condition means a module hardware alarm suppresses or masks lower-level traffic alarms from the same failed module.
concepts.example: MOD-HW is shown while derivative FRAME-LOSS alarms from the card are hidden.

concepts.label: errors appear
concepts.gloss: This condition means traffic errors are observed only at the impaired receiver.
concepts.example: One terminal reports pre-FEC errors while the peer receiver and other wavelengths remain clean.

concepts.label: stay healthy
concepts.gloss: This condition means the route and other wavelengths remain normal when a defect is confined to one receiver.
concepts.example: Only λ6 has errors at one receiver; λ5, λ7, and the fibre route test healthy.

concepts.label: The laser bias climbs as the laser ages
concepts.gloss: This condition is a gradual increase in laser bias current needed to maintain output as the laser ages.
concepts.example: Transmit bias rises from 100% to 118% of its commissioning value over a year.

concepts.label: an eventual dark transmitter
concepts.gloss: This condition is the final transmitter failure state reached after progressive laser ageing.
concepts.example: After months of rising bias, the laser stops emitting and the far end raises RX-DARK.

concepts.label: The wavelength's margin shrinks slowly
concepts.gloss: This condition means a wavelength's performance margin gradually decreases because of accumulated impairment along its route.
concepts.example: Estimated margin declines by 0.2 dB per month across the optical path.

concepts.label: it is seen
concepts.gloss: This condition means the route-wide loss of wavelength margin is observed in measurements at the receiving terminal.
concepts.example: The receiver's estimated OSNR trend reveals a margin decrease caused upstream.

concepts.label: The OTU frame is lost though light arrives
concepts.gloss: This condition is loss of OTU framing while optical light is still present at the receiver.
concepts.example: The terminal measures normal receive power but raises FRAME-LOSS because it cannot decode the OTU frame.

concepts.label: Pre-FEC errors exceed the degrade level
concepts.gloss: This condition occurs when the measured pre-FEC error rate exceeds the configured degradation threshold while framing remains available.
concepts.example: Pre-FEC BER rises above 1×10^-3 and the terminal raises DEGRADE.

concepts.label: The other end reports a defect in what this terminal sends
concepts.gloss: This condition means the far-end terminal reports a defect in the signal transmitted by the local terminal.
concepts.example: The peer detects errors on the local wavelength and returns an indication that raises REMOTE-DEFECT locally.

concepts.label: Laser bias above 120 per cent of its commissioning value
concepts.gloss: This condition occurs when transmit laser bias exceeds 120 percent of its commissioning reference value.
concepts.example: Bias reaches 123%, causing the terminal to raise TX-BIAS.

concepts.label: customer errored seconds
concepts.gloss: Customer errored seconds is a base-available tributary performance count of one-second intervals containing errors in the customer service.
concepts.example: If errors occur during 12 distinct seconds, the tributary records 12 customer errored seconds.

concepts.label: customer unavailable seconds
concepts.gloss: Customer unavailable seconds is a base-available tributary performance count of seconds during which the customer service is declared unavailable.
concepts.example: A 90-second tributary outage adds 90 customer unavailable seconds.

concepts.label: Aggregate optical power entering the module
concepts.gloss: Aggregate power in is the total optical power of all wavelengths entering an amplifier module, available with the Optical Power pack.
concepts.example: The Optical Power pack reports -4 dBm total input power across 40 channels.

concepts.label: Aggregate optical power leaving the module
concepts.gloss: Aggregate power out is the total optical power of all wavelengths leaving an amplifier module, available with the Optical Power pack.
concepts.example: The OFA reports +16 dBm aggregate output power after amplification.

concepts.label: Pump drive, as a share of the value at commissioning
concepts.gloss: Pump drive is an Insight-pack measurement expressing OFA pump current or drive as a percentage of its commissioning value.
concepts.example: A reading of 115% means the pump is driven 15% harder than at commissioning.

concepts.label: Whether the supervisory link is being received
concepts.gloss: Supervisory received is a base status indicating whether an OFA is receiving the supervisory link from the preceding fibre span.
concepts.example: The status changes to false after the supervisory fibre is cut.

concepts.label: per wavelength, the level
concepts.gloss: Per-wavelength level is a Spectrum-pack measurement of optical power separately for each wavelength at the router.
concepts.example: The router reports λ1 at -2.1 dBm and λ2 at -5.4 dBm.

concepts.label: per wavelength, the OSNR
concepts.gloss: Per-wavelength OSNR is a Spectrum-pack measurement of optical signal-to-noise ratio separately for each wavelength at the router.
concepts.example: The router reports 18 dB OSNR for λ7.

concepts.label: Received light level
concepts.gloss: Received light level is the optical power measured at a receiver and is exposed through base or Optical Power telemetry.
concepts.example: A terminal reports -12.5 dBm receive power.

concepts.label: errored seconds
concepts.gloss: Errored seconds is a base performance count of one-second intervals in which the monitored terminal signal contains one or more errors.
concepts.example: Errors in five separate seconds increment the counter by five.

concepts.label: estimated OSNR
concepts.gloss: Estimated OSNR is an Insight-pack receiver estimate of the wavelength's optical signal-to-noise ratio.
concepts.example: The terminal estimates 14.8 dB OSNR without an external spectrum analyzer.

concepts.label: pre-FEC error ratio
concepts.gloss: Pre-FEC error ratio is the Insight-pack measurement of errored bits before forward-error correction is applied.
concepts.example: The receiver reports a pre-FEC error ratio of 2×10^-4.

concepts.label: DGD
concepts.gloss: DGD is the Insight-pack measurement of differential group delay experienced by the received wavelength.
concepts.example: The coherent receiver reports 18 ps of DGD.

concepts.label: polarisation drift rate
concepts.gloss: Polarisation drift rate is the Insight-pack measurement of how quickly the received state of polarization changes.
concepts.example: A sudden increase to 50 krad/s indicates rapid polarization movement.

concepts.label: Transmit laser bias, as a share of its value at commissioning
concepts.gloss: Transmit laser bias is an Insight-pack measurement expressing laser bias current as a percentage of its commissioning reference.
concepts.example: A value of 122% accompanies a TX-BIAS alarm.

concepts.label: TRIB-FAIL
concepts.gloss: TRIB-FAIL is a tributary-port alarm raised when the customer service on that tributary has failed, with possible causes including local tributary failure, misprovisioning, or a fabric outage.
concepts.example: A failed VC-TRIB-100 optic drops service and raises TRIB-FAIL.

concepts.label: AIS-IN
concepts.gloss: AIS-IN is a tributary-port alarm indicating that ODU AIS is being received on an ODU handled by the port.
concepts.example: An upstream line failure inserts AIS, and the destination tributary raises AIS-IN.

concepts.label: REMOTE-AIS
concepts.gloss: REMOTE-AIS is a tributary-port alarm indicating that the far endpoint reports receiving ODU AIS.
concepts.example: The peer sees AIS on the transmitted ODU, so the local port raises REMOTE-AIS.

concepts.label: TRACE-MISMATCH
concepts.gloss: TRACE-MISMATCH is a tributary-port alarm indicating that the arriving ODU identity or trace does not match the expected recipient, commonly because of misprovisioning.
concepts.example: Customer B's trace arrives at customer A's port and triggers TRACE-MISMATCH.

concepts.label: ON-STANDBY
concepts.gloss: ON-STANDBY is a tributary-port alarm or status indicating that the protection selector is currently using the standby ODU route.
concepts.example: The primary route fails and the port raises ON-STANDBY after selecting route B.

concepts.label: STANDBY-LOST
concepts.gloss: STANDBY-LOST is a tributary-port alarm indicating failure of the standby ODU route and consequent loss of protection redundancy.
concepts.example: The standby route receives AIS while primary remains active, causing STANDBY-LOST.

concepts.label: TRIB-HW
concepts.gloss: TRIB-HW is a tributary-port hardware alarm that localizes a physical fault to that tributary.
concepts.example: A failed interface ASIC on VC-TRIB-400 raises TRIB-HW.

concepts.label: FABRIC-HW
concepts.gloss: FABRIC-HW is a digital-cross-connect alarm that localizes a physical hardware defect to the switching fabric.
concepts.example: A failed fabric card in the VC-DXC raises FABRIC-HW.

concepts.label: IN-DARK
concepts.gloss: IN-DARK is a mid-span OFA alarm indicating no optical light at its input, potentially due to a preceding fibre break, attenuation jump, or amplifier outage.
concepts.example: A cut before a VC-OFA-M removes its input light and raises IN-DARK.

concepts.label: SEC-IN-DARK
concepts.gloss: SEC-IN-DARK is a landing OFA alarm indicating that the wavelength section arrives with no optical light.
concepts.example: An unplugged launch-site patch lead makes the VC-OFA-R raise SEC-IN-DARK.

concepts.label: SV-LOSS
concepts.gloss: SV-LOSS is a mid-span or landing OFA alarm indicating loss of the incoming supervisory link, typically from fibre loss or excessive attenuation.
concepts.example: A span cut prevents the next shelter from receiving supervision and raises SV-LOSS.

concepts.label: OUT-DARK
concepts.gloss: OUT-DARK is an OFA alarm indicating no optical output despite optical light being present at the module input, pointing to amplifier outage.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-T has valid input power but zero output and raises OUT-DARK.

concepts.label: GAIN-DEV
concepts.gloss: GAIN-DEV is a mid-span or landing OFA alarm raised when actual gain differs from its setting by more than 2 dB.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-R set to 20 dB produces 17 dB and raises GAIN-DEV.

concepts.label: PUMP-EOL
concepts.gloss: PUMP-EOL is an OFA end-of-life alarm raised when pump drive exceeds 120 percent of its commissioning value.
concepts.example: A VC-OFA-M reaches 121% I-PUMP and raises PUMP-EOL.

concepts.label: RX-DARK
concepts.gloss: RX-DARK is a wavelength-terminal alarm indicating that its receiver detects no optical light, with possible causes anywhere from the remote transmitter through the intervening path.
concepts.example: A remote transmitter fails and the receiving VC-WT-400T raises RX-DARK.

concepts.label: FRAME-LOSS
concepts.gloss: FRAME-LOSS is a wavelength-terminal alarm indicating loss of OTU framing even though optical light is present.
concepts.example: Excess noise prevents frame synchronization while receive power remains normal, causing FRAME-LOSS.

concepts.label: DEGRADE
concepts.gloss: DEGRADE is a wavelength-terminal alarm raised when pre-FEC errors exceed the configured degradation level.
concepts.example: A dirty connector raises pre-FEC BER above threshold and the VC-WT-400A raises DEGRADE.

concepts.label: REMOTE-DEFECT
concepts.gloss: REMOTE-DEFECT is a wavelength-terminal alarm indicating that the far endpoint reports a defect in the signal sent by the local terminal.
concepts.example: The peer cannot decode the local transmission and returns a defect indication that raises REMOTE-DEFECT.

concepts.label: TX-HW
concepts.gloss: TX-HW is a wavelength-terminal alarm for a hardware fault localized to its transmit laser or laser circuitry.
concepts.example: A laser-driver failure on a VC-WT-200D raises TX-HW.

concepts.label: MOD-HW
concepts.gloss: MOD-HW is a wavelength-terminal alarm for a hardware failure of the terminal module as a whole.
concepts.example: A failed module controller stops telemetry and raises MOD-HW.

concepts.label: TX-BIAS
concepts.gloss: TX-BIAS is a wavelength-terminal ageing alarm raised when laser bias exceeds 120 percent of its commissioning value.
concepts.example: A VC-WT-400T reports 124% transmit bias and raises TX-BIAS.

concepts.label: The switching fabric
concepts.gloss: The switching-fabric scope comprises the internal digital matrix and control elements that switch ODUs within a cross-connect.
concepts.example: A fabric outage affects the matrix carrying all ODUs through VC-DXC.

concepts.label: every ODU
concepts.gloss: The every-ODU scope denotes all ODU connections traversing the relevant cross-connect rather than one selected ODU.
concepts.example: A fabric outage cuts all 40 ODUs switched at the node.

concepts.label: A connection
concepts.gloss: The connection scope is one provisioned logical mapping through the digital cross-connect.
concepts.example: The mapping from line ODU2 to tributary port 7 is one connection.

concepts.label: one ODU
concepts.gloss: The one-ODU scope limits an effect to a single Optical Data Unit rather than the full fabric or wavelength set.
concepts.example: A wrong mapping sends only customer A's ODU to the wrong destination.

concepts.label: the optical side
concepts.gloss: The optical-side scope is the wavelength and photonic transport layer outside the digital ODU switching function.
concepts.example: A DXC misconfiguration leaves optical power and line alarms normal on the optical side.

concepts.label: The customer-facing optic
concepts.gloss: The customer-facing-optic scope is the optical transceiver that connects a tributary port to customer equipment.
concepts.example: Failure of the client-side SFP affects the customer-facing optic.

concepts.label: the tributary itself
concepts.gloss: The tributary-itself scope is the tributary port's internal interface and processing hardware, excluding the wider cross-connect fabric.
concepts.example: A failed tributary ASIC affects the tributary itself.

concepts.label: the customer service
concepts.gloss: The customer-service scope is the end-user traffic service carried by the specified tributary.
concepts.example: TRIB-FAIL affects the customer's 100-Gbit/s Ethernet service.

concepts.label: the module
concepts.gloss: The module scope is the complete amplifier or terminal module whose inputs, outputs, and internal operation are under discussion.
concepts.example: An amplifier outage means nothing leaves that VC-OFA-M module.

concepts.label: every wavelength it carried
concepts.gloss: The wavelengths-carried scope comprises all optical channels that were passing through the affected amplifier.
concepts.example: Failure of an OFA removes all 32 wavelengths it carried.

concepts.label: every wavelength
concepts.gloss: The every-wavelength scope denotes all channels traversing the affected component, not merely one channel.
concepts.example: Gain sag lowers every wavelength through the amplifier.

concepts.label: Output levels
concepts.gloss: The output-levels scope comprises the measured optical powers at a module's output.
concepts.example: Output levels remain normal despite excess amplifier noise.

concepts.label: I-PUMP
concepts.gloss: The I-PUMP scope is the amplifier telemetry value representing normalized optical-pump drive.
concepts.example: Pump wear-out causes I-PUMP to creep from 100% to 120%.

concepts.label: the trend
concepts.gloss: The trend scope is the time-series progression of a monitored value rather than a single instantaneous reading.
concepts.example: The upward I-PUMP trend ends at the PUMP-EOL threshold.

concepts.label: service
concepts.gloss: The service scope is the transported customer traffic whose availability or quality may be affected.
concepts.example: Early pump wear has no effect on the carried service.

concepts.label: the wavelengths at one end of the band
concepts.gloss: The band-end-wavelength scope comprises channels near one edge of the amplifier's supported optical spectrum.
concepts.example: Spectral tilt makes the highest-frequency four channels weaker.

concepts.label: one wavelength
concepts.gloss: The one-wavelength scope limits an effect to a single optical channel independently routed through the wavelength router.
concepts.example: Passband misalignment degrades λ12 while neighboring channels remain healthy.

concepts.label: All the light coming in on that direction
concepts.gloss: The direction-light scope comprises all wavelengths entering a router through one specified directional input.
concepts.example: A west-input failure stops every channel arriving from the west.

concepts.label: light entering on the other directions
concepts.gloss: The other-direction-light scope comprises wavelengths entering the router through ingress directions other than the failed one.
concepts.example: North and east input traffic continues after the west input fails.

concepts.label: the transmit laser
concepts.gloss: The transmit-laser scope is the optical source within a wavelength terminal that generates its outgoing carrier.
concepts.example: A TX-HW defect stops the VC-WT-400T transmit laser.

concepts.label: the terminal at the other end of the wavelength
concepts.gloss: This scope is the remote wavelength terminal paired with the local terminal across the same optical channel.
concepts.example: The terminal at the other end of λ7 raises RX-DARK when the local laser fails.

concepts.label: the terminal at the other end
concepts.gloss: This scope is the peer terminal at the remote endpoint of the connection.
concepts.example: A local module failure causes the terminal at the other end to lose the transmitted wavelength.

concepts.label: what the module receives
concepts.gloss: This scope is all signal and traffic entering the receive side of the affected terminal module.
concepts.example: A MOD-HW failure discards what the module receives from the line.

concepts.label: its telemetry
concepts.gloss: The telemetry scope comprises operational measurements and status reports produced by the module.
concepts.example: Module temperature and optical-power updates stop after hardware failure.

concepts.label: its traffic alarms
concepts.gloss: The traffic-alarms scope comprises signal and service alarms derived from traffic handled by the module.
concepts.example: FRAME-LOSS is hidden while the more fundamental MOD-HW alarm is active.

concepts.label: this receiver alone
concepts.gloss: The receiver-alone scope limits an impairment and its observed errors to one terminal receiver rather than the route or transmitted signal.
concepts.example: Only the destination receiver reports errors while the route tests clean.

concepts.label: the other wavelengths
concepts.gloss: The other-wavelengths scope comprises all channels on the route except the specifically impaired wavelength.
concepts.example: λ6 is degraded, but λ1 through λ5 and λ7 remain healthy.

concepts.label: the route
concepts.gloss: The route scope is the end-to-end optical path and intervening equipment traversed by a wavelength.
concepts.example: Testing shows the route is healthy despite a fault in one receiver.

concepts.label: the laser
concepts.gloss: The laser scope is the semiconductor optical source whose ageing is reflected by increasing bias current.
concepts.example: The laser requires progressively more bias to maintain output power.

concepts.label: transmitter
concepts.gloss: The transmitter scope is the complete terminal function that generates and launches an outgoing wavelength.
concepts.example: Continued laser wear eventually leaves the transmitter dark.

concepts.label: the wavelength's margin
concepts.gloss: Wavelength margin is the remaining tolerance between current signal quality and the point at which errors or frame loss occur.
concepts.example: A wavelength with 2 dB margin can tolerate roughly 2 dB more impairment before degrading.

concepts.label: this cross-connect
concepts.gloss: This location is the particular digital cross-connect currently being monitored or diagnosed.
concepts.example: FABRIC-HW localizes the fault inside VC-DXC at the current site.

concepts.label: switched through this cross-connect
concepts.gloss: This location qualifier identifies ODUs whose path traverses the current digital cross-connect.
concepts.example: Only ODUs switched through the failed node are cut by its fabric outage.

concepts.label: on the ODU route in use
concepts.gloss: This location is the currently selected end-to-end ODU path carrying the service.
concepts.example: A fault on the ODU route in use causes the selector to choose standby.

concepts.label: at either end
concepts.gloss: This location denotes either endpoint of the ODU or wavelength connection.
concepts.example: A tributary failure at either end can drop the customer service.

concepts.label: at a cross-connect along the ODU route
concepts.gloss: This location is any digital cross-connect traversed by the service's ODU route.
concepts.example: A fabric outage at an intermediate cross-connect interrupts the routed ODU.

concepts.label: the customer service on this tributary
concepts.gloss: This location is the customer service as presented on the specifically referenced tributary port.
concepts.example: TRIB-FAIL is shown on the customer service attached to VC-TRIB-100.

concepts.label: the ODU arriving
concepts.gloss: This location is the incoming ODU at the receiving interface before it is accepted or switched.
concepts.example: Trace checking finds that the ODU arriving belongs to another customer.

concepts.label: on the primary route
concepts.gloss: This location is the preferred ODU path used under normal dual-homed operation.
concepts.example: Traffic normally travels on the primary route until a defect is detected.

concepts.label: the selector
concepts.gloss: This location is the protection-selection function that chooses between primary and standby ODU routes.
concepts.example: ON-STANDBY is displayed at the receiving tributary's selector.

concepts.label: on the standby route
concepts.gloss: This location denotes an event or condition occurring on the alternate ODU protection path.
concepts.example: AIS on the standby route causes STANDBY-LOST.

concepts.label: the standby route
concepts.gloss: This location is the alternate ODU path reserved to carry service when the primary path fails.
concepts.example: The selector moves traffic to the standby route after a primary outage.

concepts.label: this tributary
concepts.gloss: This location is the particular tributary port currently being monitored or diagnosed.
concepts.example: TRIB-HW identifies a hardware defect in this VC-TRIB-400.

concepts.label: downstream
concepts.gloss: This location denotes points reached after the affected component in the direction of signal propagation.
concepts.example: Excess amplifier noise is observed at the downstream router.

concepts.label: this module
concepts.gloss: This location is the specific amplifier or terminal module currently under observation.
concepts.example: PUMP-EOL is raised on this VC-OFA-M rather than on the preceding amplifier.

concepts.label: the fibre length feeding the module
concepts.gloss: This location is the fibre span immediately upstream of and delivering light to the module.
concepts.example: A bend in the feeding fibre weakens the OFA input.

concepts.label: the OFA before that fibre length
concepts.gloss: This location is the optical fibre amplifier upstream of the fibre span feeding the current module.
concepts.example: An outage of the previous OFA makes the current module's input dark.

concepts.label: the patch lead at the head of the wavelength section
concepts.gloss: This location is the optical jumper at the transmitting head of a wavelength section.
concepts.example: An unplugged patch lead at the section head causes SEC-IN-DARK at the far landing OFA.

concepts.label: the router
concepts.gloss: This location is the wavelength router at which a routing, attenuation, or direction-input symptom is observed.
concepts.example: The weak λ8 condition first appears at the router output.

concepts.label: the other end of the wavelength
concepts.gloss: This location is the remote endpoint of the same wavelength path.
concepts.example: A local dark transmitter is detected as no light at the other end of the wavelength.

concepts.label: the other end
concepts.gloss: This location is the remote endpoint relative to the currently observed terminal or tributary.
concepts.example: The terminal at the other end reports a defect in the locally transmitted signal.

concepts.label: on this side
concepts.gloss: This location is the local endpoint containing the module currently being diagnosed.
concepts.example: A module failure stops telemetry on this side while the peer reports wavelength loss.

concepts.label: along its route
concepts.gloss: This location spans the intervening optical path over which wavelength impairment can accumulate.
concepts.example: Margin shrinks gradually along the route through several amplifiers and routers.

concepts.label: at the receiver
concepts.gloss: This location is the receiving terminal where end-to-end wavelength quality and margin are finally observed.
concepts.example: The reduced OSNR margin is seen at the receiver.

concepts.label: anywhere earlier on the wavelength's route
concepts.gloss: This location is any upstream point on the same wavelength path before the current observation point.
concepts.example: An attenuation jump anywhere earlier on the wavelength route can cause FRAME-LOSS here.

concepts.label: Earlier on the route
concepts.gloss: This location denotes an upstream segment of the current route relative to the observing equipment.
concepts.example: Excess noise introduced earlier on the route remains visible at the terminal.

concepts.label: this terminal
concepts.gloss: This location is the wavelength terminal currently reporting or being diagnosed.
concepts.example: A receiver impairment in this terminal causes local errors only.

concepts.label: between here and the other end, the other end included
concepts.gloss: This location covers the entire path from the local endpoint through and including the remote endpoint.
concepts.example: REMOTE-DEFECT can reflect a fault anywhere between here and the other end, including the peer receiver.

concepts.label: what this terminal sends
concepts.gloss: This location identifies the outgoing signal generated by the current terminal and evaluated by the far end.
concepts.example: The peer reports a defect in what this terminal sends.

concepts.label: This terminal's transmitter
concepts.gloss: This location is the transmit section of the current wavelength terminal.
concepts.example: TX-HW localizes a laser fault to this terminal's transmitter.

concepts.label: Base
concepts.gloss: Base is the standard telemetry entitlement that exposes core status and performance measurements without an optional analytics pack.
concepts.example: A base system reports customer unavailable seconds and supervisory-received status.

concepts.label: Optical Power pack
concepts.gloss: The Optical Power pack is an optional telemetry entitlement that exposes detailed input, output, and receive optical-power measurements.
concepts.example: Enabling the pack adds aggregate OFA input and output power readings.

concepts.label: Insight pack
concepts.gloss: The Insight pack is an optional analytics entitlement providing derived health and impairment metrics such as OSNR, DGD, pump drive, and laser bias.
concepts.example: With Insight enabled, an operator trends estimated OSNR and normalized laser bias.

concepts.label: With the Spectrum pack
concepts.gloss: The Spectrum pack is an optional capability that provides per-wavelength spectral measurements at a wavelength router.
concepts.example: The pack reports individual level and OSNR values for each channel through VC-WR-X.

concepts.label: An outage.
concepts.gloss: Outage is a fault nature in which the affected resource or service becomes unavailable rather than merely degraded.
concepts.example: A dark transmitter causes a complete wavelength outage.

concepts.label: An outage; it happens mostly straight after provisioning work.
concepts.gloss: Provisioning outage is service unavailability caused by incorrect configuration and therefore most likely immediately after provisioning work.
concepts.example: A newly changed DXC mapping sends an ODU to the wrong port and drops service.

concepts.label: A degradation.
concepts.gloss: Degradation is a fault nature in which service remains present but quality, power, margin, or reliability is reduced.
concepts.example: Excess amplifier noise lowers OSNR and raises errors without immediately dropping traffic.

concepts.label: Slow
concepts.gloss: Slow is a temporal fault nature describing gradual evolution over an extended period rather than a sudden event.
concepts.example: Laser bias climbs over months during transmitter wear-out.

concepts.label: urgent
concepts.gloss: Urgent is a severity classification requiring prompt operational response because service is lost or at immediate risk.
concepts.example: RX-DARK on an in-service wavelength is treated as urgent.

concepts.label: information only
concepts.gloss: Information only is a non-action severity used for state indications that inform operators without identifying a fault requiring repair.
concepts.example: ON-STANDBY may be logged as information only after successful protection switching.

concepts.label: important
concepts.gloss: Important is a severity classification for a significant condition that merits attention but is less immediately critical than an urgent outage.
concepts.example: STANDBY-LOST is important because service remains up but redundancy is gone.

concepts.label: advisory
concepts.gloss: Advisory is a low-priority severity for early warning or maintenance conditions that do not yet materially affect service.
concepts.example: PUMP-EOL is advisory while traffic remains healthy but pump replacement should be planned.

concepts.label: dual-homed, with a primary and a standby ODU route and the selector at the receiving tributary
concepts.gloss: Dual-homed routing is the protection behavior in which a service has primary and standby ODU routes and a selector at the receiving tributary chooses the usable route.
concepts.example: When the primary ODU receives AIS, the destination tributary switches to the clean standby route with only a brief interruption.

concepts.label: The router steers every wavelength on its own as it leaves a direction.
concepts.gloss: Router routing is the behavior by which a wavelength router independently steers each wavelength from an ingress direction to its selected egress.
concepts.example: From one west input, the router sends λ1 north, λ2 east, and λ3 south.
